steps.tx: International guidelines establish differing diagnostic thresholds for **gestational diabetes**. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (**NICE**) diagnoses gestational diabetes when fasting plasma glucose is at least 5.6 mmol/L (100 mg/dL) or 2-hour 75 g OGTT glucose is at least 7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL). Conversely, **IADPSG** criteria derived from the **HAPO** study diagnose GDM if any single threshold is met: fasting >=92, 1-hour >=180, or 2-hour >=153 mg/dL.
steps.say: Diagnostic criteria for gestational diabetes differ across international bodies. NICE guidelines diagnose gestational diabetes with fasting glucose at or above 5.6 mmol/L or two-hour OGTT glucose at or above 7 point 8 mmol/L. In contrast, IADPSG criteria from the HAPO trial diagnose diabetes if any single threshold is exceeded: fasting 92, one-hour 180, or two-hour 153 mg/dL.

steps.tx: The Diabetes in Pregnancy Study Group India (**DIPSI**) protocol represents the single-step national programme screening test utilized across India. In the DIPSI procedure, a non-fasting oral challenge of 75 grams of anhydrous glucose is administered to the pregnant woman regardless of the timing of her last meal. A 2-hour venous plasma glucose of **140 mg/dL** or higher establishes the diagnosis of **gestational diabetes** in routine primary healthcare settings.
steps.say: The DIPSI protocol is the non-fasting Indian national screening test for gestational diabetes. A seventy-five gram oral glucose load is administered regardless of prior meal timing, and a two-hour venous plasma glucose at or above 140 mg/dL confirms gestational diabetes in resource-appropriate clinical settings.

left.title: DIPSI Single-Step Test
points: Non-fasting 75 g oral glucose load administered
Single blood draw at 2 hours post-load
Diagnostic threshold: >=140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L)
High compliance in ambulatory Indian antenatal clinics

right.title: IADPSG / WHO Two-Hour OGTT
points: Requires mandatory overnight 8 to 10 hour fast
Three blood draws: fasting, 1 hour, and 2 hours
Thresholds: 92 mg/dL fasting, 180 at 1 hr, 153 at 2 hr
Higher sensitivity but requires multiple timed phlebotomies

steps.tx: When nutritional and lifestyle modifications fail to maintain target glycaemia in gestational diabetes within 1 to 2 weeks, pharmacological intervention is indicated. Under **NICE** guidance, oral **metformin** may be offered as initial medical therapy, adding **insulin** if glycemic targets are not attained or if metformin is not tolerated. In contrast, American Diabetes Association guidelines recommend insulin as the preferred first-line agent, noting that metformin readily crosses the placenta.
steps.say: When medical nutrition therapy fails to achieve glycemic control in gestational diabetes, pharmacotherapy is required. NICE guidelines permit starting oral metformin before adding insulin. Conversely, the American Diabetes Association prefers insulin as first-line therapy because metformin crosses the human placenta.

rows: Approved as first-line oral medical option
Metformin reserved if insulin is unfeasible

steps.tx: Rigorous self-monitoring of blood glucose is essential throughout **pregnancy**. American Diabetes Association consensus establishes strict glycaemic targets for gestational diabetes and preexisting diabetes: **fasting glucose** strictly below 95 mg/dL (5.3 mmol/L), 1-hour postprandial glucose below 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L), and 2-hour postprandial glucose below 120 mg/dL (6.7 mmol/L). Doses of prandial and basal insulin are systematically titrated to meet these targets.
steps.say: Self-monitoring targets during pregnancy require tight control to minimize adverse neonatal outcomes. The American Diabetes Association recommends maintaining fasting glucose below 95 mg/dL, one-hour postprandial glucose below 140 mg/dL, and two-hour postprandial glucose below 120 mg/dL throughout gestation.

steps.tx: Preconception care for women with **pregestational diabetes** targets an HbA1c as close to 6.5% as feasible without severe hypoglycemia, high-dose folic acid (5 mg daily), and immediate cessation of teratogenic **ACE inhibitors**, receptor blockers, and statins. Uncontrolled first-trimester hyperglycaemia markedly elevates the risk of major congenital malformations, most characteristically **caudal regression** syndrome (sacral agenesis), ventricular septal defects, transposition of the great arteries, and neural tube defects.
steps.say: Preconception counseling in pregestational diabetes emphasizes achieving an HbA1c below 6.5% and stopping teratogenic medications such as ACE inhibitors and statins. Early first-trimester hyperglycemia significantly increases the risk of severe congenital anomalies, classically caudal regression syndrome and cardiac structural defects.

steps.tx: Persistent maternal hyperglycemia during the second and third trimesters delivers excess glucose across the placenta into fetal circulation, stimulating fetal pancreatic hypertrophy and massive insulin hypersecretion. Fetal hyperinsulinemia acts as a potent growth factor, producing asymmetric fetal **macrosomia** with shoulder dystocia, fetal polycythaemia from tissue hypoxia, organomegaly, and severe **neonatal hypoglycemia** within the first hours of birth as maternal glucose supply is abruptly severed.
steps.say: Maternal hyperglycemia in the second and third trimesters stimulates fetal hyperinsulinemia. Fetal insulin acts as a powerful anabolic growth hormone, leading to macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, and severe neonatal hypoglycemia immediately following umbilical cord clamping.

left.title: Maternal-Fetal Exchange
points: Maternal glucose traverses placenta via GLUT-1
Maternal insulin cannot traverse placenta
Unchecked fetal hyperglycaemic exposure
Hypertrophy of fetal pancreatic islet beta cells

right.title: Neonatal Complications
points: Macrosomia (birth weight >4000 to 4500 g)
Birth trauma and shoulder dystocia
Profound rebound neonatal hypoglycemia
Neonatal polycythemia, jaundice, respiratory distress

steps.tx: Following delivery, placental expulsion causes an abrupt collapse of human placental lactogen and progesterone levels, resulting in rapid restoration of maternal insulin sensitivity. Women diagnosed with gestational diabetes must undergo a definitive 75 g 2-hour **OGTT** at 4 to 12 weeks **postpartum** to screen for persistent dysglycemia. Even if postpartum testing is normal, these women carry a 50% lifetime risk of developing type 2 diabetes.
steps.say: After delivery, insulin resistance is cleared rapidly with expulsion of the placenta. Women with gestational diabetes should undergo a seventy-five gram oral glucose tolerance test four to twelve weeks postpartum to assess for persistent diabetes, followed by lifelong regular screening given their high risk of developing type 2 diabetes.

steps.tx: The multicenter randomized **CONCEPTT** trial demonstrated that incorporating real-time **continuous glucose monitoring** in pregnant women with **type 1 diabetes** significantly improved neonatal outcomes compared with standard capillary glucose monitoring. Pregnant women utilizing CGM spent significantly more time in pregnancy-specific target range (63 to 140 mg/dL), which directly translated into reduced rates of large-for-gestational-age infants, fewer neonatal intensive care admissions, and reduced neonatal hypoglycemia.
steps.say: The CONCEPTT trial demonstrated that real-time continuous glucose monitoring in pregnant women with type 1 diabetes significantly improves neonatal outcomes. Mothers utilizing CGM spent more time in the tight pregnancy target range, resulting in fewer large-for-gestational-age infants and reduced neonatal intensive care admissions.

left.title: Capillary Self-Monitoring
points: Intermittent fingerstick capillary checks (4 to 7 daily)
Misses asymptomatic nocturnal hypoglycemic events
Lower total maternal time in target range
Higher rate of large-for-gestational-age infants

right.title: CONCEPTT Real-Time CGM
points: Continuous 24-hour sensor glucose monitoring
Pregnancy target range: 63 to 140 mg/dL (3.5 to 7.8 mmol/L)
Significant absolute reduction in neonatal hypoglycemia
Reduces neonatal intensive care length of stay
